lines.text: How much fits in one second? Here's one. A kitchen. A window. Coffee on the table. A fly crosses the room, and it's over. You barely noticed it. Now I'll play that same second again, slower. And then slower again, and again, and again. I won't stop until light itself looks like it's standing still. On the way, we'll watch wings, a splash, a pop, a bullet, and a bolt of lightning. Each one hides something that's too fast to see.

lines.text: Ten times slower. One second now takes ten. A small hummingbird hovers at the window. Its wings beat about fifty times a second. At ten times slower, that's five beats a second. Now you can see them. Not a blur anymore, just wings, going up and down. Here's why they blur at full speed. Your eyes blend flashes that come faster than about sixty a second. So fifty wing beats a second just smear together. Now the fly. A housefly beats its wings about two hundred times a second. Slow it a hundred times, and that's two beats a second. One second now lasts almost two minutes. The fly's wing sweeps forward, flips over, and sweeps back. All of that was hiding inside one blink. A mosquito's wings beat about five hundred times a second. At a hundred times slower, that's five beats a second. You can count them on one hand.

lines.text: Now, someone claps at the far end of the kitchen. Sound is air pushing on air. In a room, it moves about three hundred forty meters a second. That's why you never see it travel. It reaches the wall, and bounces back. You use this trick in every storm. Sound covers about a kilometer in three seconds. So count the seconds between a flash and its thunder, and divide by three. That's roughly how many kilometers away the lightning is.

lines.text: Ten thousand times slower. One second now lasts almost three hours. A famous old photograph by Harold Edgerton shows a bullet going through an apple. That bullet flew at about eight hundred fifty meters a second. The apple is about eight centimeters across. So the bullet crosses it in less than a ten-thousandth of a second. Here, that takes about one second. The skin dimples. Then the back of the apple blows outward, in a spray. And the bullet is already past. It's moving more than twice as fast as sound, so it drags a narrow cone of air behind it. Even now, a table a meter wide would take it about twelve seconds to cross. And a clap across the room would still take about two and a half minutes to arrive.

lines.text: A million times slower. One second now lasts twelve days. Beyond the window, a storm. Lightning looks like it strikes in an instant. It doesn't. The whole fall from the cloud takes tens of thousandths of a second. At this speed, that would take hours. So I'll skip ahead, and show you the highlights. First, a faint path of electric charge reaches down from the cloud, in jumps. Each jump is tens of meters long. Each takes about a microsecond. Here, one jump lasts one whole second. Then the path waits, about thirty to fifty microseconds. Here, that's half a minute or more. Then it jumps again, feeling its way down. At last it touches the ground, and a bright flash runs back up the three-kilometer path. That flash travels up to about a third of the speed of light. Even at a million times slower, it takes at least thirty seconds to climb.

lines.text: Now it gets strange. Ten million times slower. One second now lasts about one hundred sixteen days. A whole season fits inside it. A hundred million times slower, and one second lasts more than three years. At this speed, a flash of light would take almost two seconds to cross the room. And the chip in your phone would tick thirty times a second. Now we're close. Everything you've seen so far happened in less than a second of real time. And all of it was hiding in plain sight.

lines.text: A billion times slower. One second now lasts about thirty-two years. Now the light itself is slow. Light moves about thirty centimeters in a billionth of a second. So at this speed, it crawls thirty centimeters in one second. That's a slow crawl. Someone flicks on a flashlight. The beam is not instant anymore. A glowing front of light leaves the lens, and spreads across the room. Behind it, the table is lit. Ahead of it, the table is still dark. The cup lights up on one side first, and its shadow arrives last. It takes about seventeen seconds to reach the far wall. In real time, that crossing takes about seventeen billionths of a second. And the chip in the corner? A computer chip ticks about three billion times a second. Here, it ticks three times a second. Tick. Tick. Tick. Even the chip in your phone is slow enough to count.

lines.text: Keep going. Ten billion times slower. Now, light moves three centimeters a second. A hundred billion, and it moves three millimeters a second. The room would take about four and a half hours to cross. Here's another way to see it. A human hair is about a tenth of a millimeter wide. lines.text: This isn't just a story. A team at MIT built a camera that records about a trillion frames a second. They used it to film a pulse of light moving through a bottle.
